design_notes: Requirement 1 needed no core change at all: ArgType (accepts/schema/describe) plus Registry(arg_types=...)/add_type already existed from the first round, so the plug-in is one new file handed to the constructor. A test asserts the plug-in's imports are exactly {re, ..argtypes} and that registry.py, binder.py, records.py, describe.py, diagnose.py, walker.py, phrases.py and argtypes.py contain neither 'rgb' nor 'set_color', so the 'local addition' claim is checked rather than asserted.

The only judgement call in requirement 1 was the tool schema: a purist would emit type 'string'. The requirement says the schema must describe the argument with type rgb, so the plug-in's schema emits "type": "rgb" plus "json_type": "string", the ECMA pattern and examples; controls get type 'rgb' for free because Describer reads spec.type.

Bug caught by the new tests and worth noting: `^#[0-9a-fA-F]{6}$` accepts a trailing newline in Python, so rgb accepts used `fullmatch`; a value like '#ff0000\n' is now refused. The type is also case-insensitive as required and rejects named colours, short hex, whitespace and non-strings without coercion.

Requirement 2 forced the one core edit: the API is `reg.voice_phrases()`, so Registry gained a three-line delegation to hubreg/phrases.py, exactly like the existing describer/walker attributes. Everything phrase-shaped lives outside the core.

Phrase generation is template-based over data every record already has: verb and object from the name (underscores to words), device kind for the '... on the <kind>' form (skipped when redundant), values from default/enum values/typical-unit midpoints/type-schema examples, and the argument doc as a spoken object only for required arguments and only when the sentence is short and free of quotes, brackets or punctuation. That guard keeps 'Colour as '\''#rrggbb'\''' out of speech while still using 'Target temperature for the room' -> 'set the target temperature for the room to 20 °C'. Enumeration values get their own phrase ('run the morning scene') rather than a clumsy 'to morning'.

Requirement 3 was easy structurally (record + option redirect, validated at registration) and hard in one respect: the chapter says a near-miss should be repaired, but a rename can be implemented either as a silent alias or as a refusal plus a fix. I chose refusal with fix='thermostat.set_temperature(temperature=21)', which is exactly what the old demo redirect machinery already produced once the redirect key became the old name; the binder needed no change, and the CLI's value coercion follows the redirect so the fix is a runnable call.

Requirement 3 also ripples through every consumer for free (schemas, controls, help, phrases, walk, CLI) because they all read the record; the only cost was updating tests that had hard-coded the old name.
chapter_feedback: Note 6 ('make argument types pluggable before they multiply') paid off exactly as promised: adding rgb was a 60-line plug-in file and zero binder edits, and the same interface made the type appear in schemas, controls, help and phrases automatically.

The chapter's insistence that every consumer read the records is what made requirements 1 and 3 cheap; it is silent, though, on generated natural-language surface forms, so the phrase templates, the doc-phrase guard and the choice of example values are my design, not the chapter's.

The chapter describes redirects from the caller's point of view ('a redirect beats the nearest name') but not the shape of a renamed *option*: ArgSpec.redirects is specified as {wrong_option: right_option} in TASK.md, yet the chapter's example ({ min } -> use above) suggests the spec that owns the redirect is the *old* option's neighbour. I kept the TASK.md reading (the new spec lists the old names) and validated targets as existing option names.

The chapter never says whether a renamed operation/option should keep working as an alias. 'Nothing falls back to a default silently' and the repairable-refusal idea point at refusal plus fix, so that is what I did; an explicit sentence on aliases versus redirects would remove the guess.

Note 8 ('rename with a redirect from the old name, validate redirects at registration') was the single most useful instruction for requirement 3 — the validation caught a self-referential redirect during development.

A fifth consumer (voice) is not in the chapter's list of participants, and its 'consumers read records' advice does not say how far a generated surface may go (only names? or prose?). It left the quality bar of generated phrases to me; a note on how the Editor lab generated labels would have helped.
